title: Children of Time
author: Tchaikovsky, Adrian
review:
I don't want to over praise this book due to recency bias, but it's good. Really good. I think it will be cemented for me as a science fiction classic. Tchaikovsky explores a lot of interesting ideas with nuance and care. Nothing seems ham-fisted and both sides of the conflict or differing philosophies are fairly represented and have you empathizing with both sides which is not easy to pull off.

This also is one of the best if not the absolute best description of aliens I have read. His zoological background makes the encounters and progression of the aliens pretty mind bending and engaging. Feels very realistic and plausible that if the cast of the evolutionary dice were different it could have ended up like this instead.

highlights.text: Sleep for a long, lonely time. She would return to the tomb, and a simulacrum of herself would stand watch over a silent planet, in a silent universe, as the last outpost of the great spacefaring human civilization.
There is no returning to Earth, he sent to the pensively silent satellite. In the end, we could not counterbalance the increasing toxicity of the environment. So we built the ark ships.

I have seen what you are. You are not from my Earth. You are not my humanity. You are monkeys, nothing but monkeys. You are not even my monkeys. My monkeys are undergoing uplift, the great experiment. They are pure.
Negotiations with the locals have gone sufficiently well—now that Portia and her party have established their superiority—
Her descendants will tell the story of how Portia entered the temple of the ants and stole the eye of their god.
Her world is one in which there is no great divide between the thinkers and the thoughtless, only a long continuum.
Who knows what we might have achieved, had we not been so keen to recreate all their follies, he thought now. Could we have saved the Earth? Would we be living there now on our own green planet?

There is nothing about what we do that is natural. If we prized the natural we would still be hunting Spitters in the wilderness, or falling prey to the jaws of ants, instead of mastering our world. We have made a virtue of the unnatural.
Your purpose is to survive and grow and prosper and to seek to understand, just as my people should have taken these things as their purpose, had they not fallen into foolishness, and perished.
At last the spiders appreciate that, even aside from their orbiting God, they are not alone in the universe, and that this is not a good thing.
What is it like to be you? A question nobody can step far enough out of their own frame of reference to answer.
“Machines, they’re just machines. Machines of a dead technology. That’s all they can be. Biological weapons.” “Who the fuck would make giant spiders as biological weapons?”

If there had been some tiny bead present in the brain of all humans, that had told each other, They are like you; that had drawn some thin silk thread of empathy, person to person, in a planet-wide net—what might then have happened? Would there have been the same wars, massacres, persecutions and crusades?
After all the years, the wars, the tragedies and the loss, the spiders and the monkeys are returning to the stars to seek their inheritance.
